name: Gilgamesh Retold (Carcanet Classics)
date: Published 25 October 2018 by Carcanet Press, Manchester (paperback ISBN 9781784106140, ebook 9781784106157, 136 pp.). Audiobook read by Lewis (ISBN 9781784108779, 2019), Carcanet's first audiobook. Written 2013 to 2018 as the creative component of a Goldsmiths PhD; the accompanying thesis, 'Translating Epic from an Unfamiliar Language', was completed March 2021.
creator: Jenny Lewis, Anglo-Welsh poet, playwright and songwriter who teaches poetry at Oxford (University of Oxford continuing education). Editor at Carcanet/Oxford Poets: Robyn Marsack. Carcanet's publisher Michael Schmidt later discussed the book at length in his own Gilgamesh: The Life of a Poem (Princeton, 2019).
form: Verse retelling that Lewis calls 'a response' rather than a translation. Prologue, fifteen titled chapters (1 'The Coming of Enkidu' to 15 'Homecoming'), Epilogue, and a prose Afterword, plus a preface, list of characters, glossary of Babylonian words and a map. Each chapter uses a different verse form, meant to represent different voices retelling the tale over millennia: alliterative/four-beat quatrains with a marked caesura, ottava rima, terza rima, blank verse, dimeter with sung/chanted passages, a specular (mirror) lament, and polyphonic 'script' chapters.
translator_access: No direct access to the cuneiform. Her thesis says plainly: 'as I am unable to decipher cuneiform or to read Babylonian, I based my book Gilgamesh Retold mainly on the scholarly translation by the Assyriologist Andrew George' (Penguin, 1999/2003). In 2012 she tried transliterating the Prologue herself using Martin Worthington's Complete Babylonian, produced a few rough lines, and abandoned the method as 'a fruitless task, resulting in a version like many others'. She then worked, like Ferry, Morgan, Chapman and Pope, 'by studying previous translations and related texts'.
scholarly_adviser: No formal crib-supplier. Primary source is Andrew George's Penguin translation, and George is thanked in the thesis acknowledgements. Other named influences: Samuel Noah Kramer (History Begins at Sumer; Wolkstein and Kramer's Inanna), Fran Hazelton of the Enheduanna Society (Three Kings of Warka), Theodore Ziolkowski (Gilgamesh Among Us), and the Iraqi poet-translator Dr Salah Niazi, who shaped her sense of cinematic perspective and approved the word 'souls' in the Shamhat scene. Iraqi poet Adnan Al-Sayegh was her long-term collaborator on the parallel 'Writing Mesopotamia' project.
versions_used: Principally the Standard Babylonian eleven-tablet epic as translated by George, whose Tablet VI placement of the Ishtar/Inanna episode she mirrors in her chiastic structure. She compared Foster (Norton) and consulted Sandars, Speiser, Gardner and Maier, Dalley, Kovacs and others. She deliberately reaches back to Sumerian material and context: Inanna replaces Ishtar as Uruk's goddess, the Prologue adds the Tiamat/Abzu creation myth, Enkidu's funeral draws on Sumerian underworld beliefs, Inanna's ascent inverts the Sumerian Descent of Inanna, and Siduri speaks in emesal (the Sumerian 'women's language'). Her thesis discusses the Sulaymaniyah Tablet V (George and Al-Rawi, 2014) but there is no evidence it was worked into the book. [uncertain]
non_standard_material: Silent merge, with explanation deferred to the Afterword. Sumerian elements, invented scenes and lines from Arabic and modern sources sit inside the verse without any typographic marking. Additions Lewis names: a new terza rima dialogue between Shamhat and Enkidu in the forest (inserted partly to balance the chiastic form); an expanded ascent of Inanna to heaven; Shamash's motive to 'equal great Inanna'; Bibbu the butcher and the underworld 'wise-women, cleaners and sweepers' at the funeral; and a 'redemption' passage in Chapter 14 that she admits is a Judeo-Christian anachronism added 'to give the tale an ending that a contemporary readership would expect'. Cuts include the trapper's father's coarse advice about Shamhat, and Gilgamesh's 47-line insult to Ishtar condensed to 24 lines. The Cannonball Read reviewer complained that the multiple-voice scheme was 'only explained in the afterword'.
gap_policy: Smoothed over. Working from George's reading translation, Lewis prioritised 'the momentum of the story' and public performance over textual fidelity, and her chapters read as continuous narrative. Where the source is most broken (Enkidu's delirious deathbed speech in Tablet VIII, 'effectively broken up by many lacunae') she turned the fragmentation into a stylistic effect, an impressionistic polyphonic soundscape of fading consciousness, rather than showing the damage. [uncertain: no line-by-line check of the book was possible]
typography_of_absence: No editorial brackets or marked lacunae. Ellipses and white space do appear, but as dramatic devices: in Chapter 9 ('The Death of Enkidu') staggered, indented lines such as '... it is almost beyond hearing' represent ebbing consciousness, and a vertical bar '|' marks the caesura in the quatrain chapters. Absence is converted into sound and layout rather than acknowledged as loss. [uncertain]
tablet_xii: Dropped from the narrative. The book ends with Chapter 15 'Homecoming' and an Epilogue that mirrors the Prologue, closing on 'Gilgamesh knew. / He understood.' Her thesis summarises Tablet XII only as scholarly background ('a late and inorganic appendage'). Whether the Afterword discusses it is not confirmed. [uncertain]
turning_point: Structurally, Chapter 8 'Inanna and Gilgamesh', the rejection of the goddess. Lewis laid the chapter summaries out on the floor and built a chiastic book with this scene 'at the dead centre', mirroring its place in Tablet VI of George's eleven-tablet version with five tablets to follow. Chapters 7 and 9 (Humbaba's killing, Enkidu's death) mirror each other as polyphonic scripts; 6 and 10 both use repetition; 5 and 11 are both dimeter with sung passages; 4 and 12 blank verse; 3 and 13 terza rima; 2 and 14 ottava rima; 1 and 15 caesura quatrains; the Prologue and Epilogue form one specular poem. The hinge lines are Inanna's curse 'You! You're only two thirds god! / I'll strike the part of you that's human' (p. 71). Lewis explains: had he been wholly divine he would be immortal, and his one-third humanity 'propels the narrative of the rest of the epic'. Enkidu's death is therefore the goddess's revenge, not an arbitrary decree, which puts a woman's wounded power at the story's centre.
arc_interpretation: Maturity and repentance, read through a feminist lens. Lewis calls the epic 'a rite of passage which questions the value of the heroic in favour of the importance of learning, acquiring wisdom and understanding, and being able to change'. Her ending makes that explicit: in Chapter 14 Gilgamesh must 'acknowledge his mistakes before he can repent and ask forgiveness from the deities he has offended', and only then 'assume the mantle of a chastened and more responsible leader'. The women drive that arc. The Cannonball Read review notes that 'without them helping him along he would not have made it'. Ninsun gets her own chanted chapter, Siduri becomes a veiled folktale guide speaking emesal, and Inanna is given more dignity: the narrator frames Gilgamesh's insults as gratuitous ('Like a shower of stones his insults hit') and has Shamash seize the moment to 'equal great Inanna', reading the episode as the shift from matriarchy to patriarchy. Lewis's framing in 2013 was also political: 'tyranny, hubris, irresponsibility of leaders and destruction of forests'. She says she did not set out to write a 'feminist version per se' but to rebalance 'the masculine and feminine energies of the original'.
key_passages: Shamhat and Enkidu: the most rewritten scene. Shamhat is cast as a hierodule (holy priestess), not a street prostitute; the trapper's father's coarse instructions are cut; the sex is tender and it is Enkidu who gentles her 'like an animal', a reversal of the usual seduction: 'Stroking her hair | like the fur of an animal / Stroking her thighs | like the flanks of an animal / As he caressed her | he sang to her softly.' It closes with 'Inanna looked down | blessing the lovers / Six nights, seven days | their bodies were joined / ... Six days, seven nights | their souls were one soul.' Lewis says the switch of singer 'shows how deeply uncomfortable I felt about this episode'. Siduri's advice: Chapter 12 'Gilgamesh at the Edge of the World', the first chapter she wrote in blank verse, in a mainly Anglo-Saxon register; Siduri is a demi-goddess 'shrouded in veils' who speaks emesal. [uncertain: exact wording of the carpe diem speech not seen] Death in the bedchamber (Tablet XI): in Chapter 13, terza rima; no wording located. [uncertain] Walls of Uruk: the SB closing tour is replaced by the Epilogue, a condensed mirror of the Prologue ending 'Gilgamesh knew. / He understood.' The Prologue reinterprets 'He who saw the Deep' as 'He who knew how the world began', and uses alliterative half-lines: 'He sensed secrets / guarded by gods / wandered wide / told a tale'. Humbaba: Joan Acocella called Lewis's account of the murder 'the nastiest I know'.
diction_and_metre: Deliberately polymetric, so every chapter changes form. Unrhymed four-beat quatrains with a marked caesura, echoing Anglo-Saxon alliterative verse, frame the book (Prologue, chapters 1 and 15). Blank verse in iambic pentameter for chapters 4 and 12 ('the easiest storytelling mode'); ottava rima (2, 14) and terza rima (3, 13), which she found hardest; dimeter with chant and plainsong-style call and response (5, 11); a specular lament modelled on the Song of Songs (10); polyphonic 'scripts' for Humbaba's death and Enkidu's (7, 9). The idiom is modern British and performable, with terse Anglo-Saxon diction modelled on Ted Hughes's Tales from Ovid ('A bolus of everything, but / As if aborted' was her benchmark). There is little archaism and heavy use of alliteration and repetition, though repetition is rationed to keep the story moving. Schmidt describes 'a gapped or sprung phrasal line'.
sample_line: "You! You're only two thirds god! / I'll strike the part of you that's human" (Inanna to Gilgamesh, Chapter 8 'Inanna and Gilgamesh', Gilgamesh Retold, p. 71; the fulcrum line of the book's chiastic structure)
critical_response: Warm, from mainly UK literary outlets. Gavin Francis, New Statesman Books of the Year 2018: 'innovative, graceful, erudite and utterly unputdownable'. London Review of Books Bookshop Book of the Week (October 2018): 'marvellous new version'. Joan Acocella, 'How to Read Gilgamesh', The New Yorker (7 October 2019): 'very musical, with rhymes and chimes and shifting meters', with 'the nastiest' Humbaba killing, yet 'the most tender, the most tragic, the one, I think, that might be recommended by feminist scholars'. Hetta Howes, TLS (21 December 2018): 'vivid, even cinematic', engaging the source 'on a "subliminal level"' rather than as a historical artefact, in the tradition of Angela Carter. David Cooke, London Grip (2019): 'essential reading' for its 'magisterial synthesis' and 'impressive variety of metrical forms'. Theophilus Kwek, The North: 'daring and deliberate approach to formal experimentation'. Poetry Book Society Winter Bulletin 2018 selection. Theodore Ziolkowski: a 'spirited "response" of a contemporary poet to the original'. Michael Schmidt (Gilgamesh: The Life of a Poem, 2019) credits it with giving Enkidu more agency but calls the Shamhat scene 'fanciful', saying 'The sacramental should not play out in quite this way'.
controversies: No accuracy or provenance scandal, but three live disputes. First, liberty: her Shamhat scene, with Inanna blessing the lovers and 'souls' joined, was criticised by Michael Schmidt as 'fanciful', and it runs against Stephen Mitchell's warning to bypass 'female indignation' when reading Shamhat. Lewis replies that most versions fail to bypass 'male lubricity'. Second, she admits the Chapter 14 redemption passage is an anachronism taken from Judeo-Christian morality. Third, the Sumerian-matriarchy framing (equal status of women, emesal as 'women's language') rests on contested scholarship; Lewis herself notes that what emesal actually was is unknown. A possible conflict of interest is worth flagging: Schmidt, the most extended critic, is also the head of Carcanet, her publisher. [uncertain: no formal Assyriological review located]
regional_reception: Unusually strong link to Iraq for an English version. Through 'Writing Mesopotamia' (Arts Council England funded, from 2012) with exiled Iraqi poet Adnan Al-Sayegh, extracts were translated into Arabic, dramatised and performed. The Flood episode appeared as a dual-language English/Arabic chapbook (Arabic by Ruba Abughaida and Al-Sayegh, woodcuts by Frances Kiernan, Mulfran Press 2017) and was exhibited at the Humanitarian Dialogue Foundation of Iraq and the Iraqi Embassy in London (April 2017). Their song 'Anthem for Gilgamesh' reportedly passed 100,000 views on YouTube and Arab websites. Al-Sayegh endorsed the book: 'poetry is the best way to rekindle the past'. Lewis won Goldsmiths' 2016 Warden's Prize for Innovation in Public Engagement for this work. No full Arabic or Kurdish translation of the book was found. [uncertain]
ai_craft_tension: Lewis is the clearest case of a poet who tried the machine-like route first and gave it up. In 2012 she sat down with a Babylonian grammar and produced word-by-word glosses ('Who sees/saw everything, land foundations / Proper ways knows entirety he understands'), then concluded that finding 'slight alternatives for some words' would only give 'a version like many others'. That is roughly what a translation model yields: a competent gloss with synonyms swapped. Everything distinctive in her book came from decisions no parallel corpus contains. She laid the chapters out on a floor to build a mirror structure around Inanna's curse, and chose a different verse form for each chapter to stand for different tellers over millennia. She rewrote the Shamhat scene because, as a woman, she could not accept the received version. She also took a word ('souls') from a conversation with an Iraqi poet, and tested lines in front of live audiences with oud music. The cost is the same as with other poets' versions. The gaps, the tablet numbering and the line between Sumerian, Babylonian and Lewis herself disappear, and she openly adds a Christian-flavoured redemption. Against Armitage, whose version rests on Jacob Dahl's philology, Lewis shows what a poet does with one scholar's translation and no crib: the value is in the rebalancing and the form, not in any new access to the text.
essay_hooks: 1) The abandoned gloss: her own 2012 attempt at Akkadian, 'Who sees/saw everything, land foundations / Proper ways knows entirety he understands', set beside George's 'He who saw the Deep, the country's foundation' (Lewis thesis, Goldsmiths 2021, pp. 71 to 72). A neat stand-in for raw machine output. 2) 'As I am unable to decipher cuneiform or to read Babylonian...' (thesis introduction): honest about the crib, unlike some predecessors. 3) Built on the floor: she laid chapter summaries out on A3 paper with Inanna's curse 'You're only two thirds god!' at the 'dead centre' (thesis p. 79). 4) The singer swap: in her Shamhat scene it is Enkidu who sings to Shamhat, which she says 'shows how deeply uncomfortable I felt about this episode' (thesis p. 88). 5) Acocella's double verdict: 'the nastiest' Humbaba killing, yet 'the most tender, the most tragic' version (New Yorker, 7 October 2019). 6) Fifteen chapters, roughly ten verse forms, one Epilogue ending 'Gilgamesh knew. / He understood.' 7) The Flood chapter went back to Iraq in Arabic and was shown at the Iraqi Embassy in London in 2017. 8) Same publisher, same year: Carcanet also issued Philip Terry's 'Globish' Dictator in 2018, two radically opposed Gilgameshes from one list.
